chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## A Company Remade

In the fourth quarter of 2025, Nebius Group's core AI cloud segment grew 802% year-on-year. Total group revenue for the quarter reached $227.7 million — itself a 547% increase over the prior-year period — and the company exited the year with an annualised revenue run-rate of $1.25 billion and $3.7 billion in cash on its balance sheet. These are not the numbers of a company finding its footing; they are the numbers of a company attempting to compress a decade of infrastructure build into roughly eighteen months.

Nebius Group N.V. trades on the NASDAQ under the ticker NBIS. It is incorporated in the Netherlands and files with the SEC on a 20-F foreign-private-issuer basis, supplemented by 6-K quarterly disclosures. Its chief executive is Arkady Volozh, who founded the company that became Yandex in 2000, led it through its 2011 NASDAQ listing and its years as Russia's dominant internet group, stepped down in 2022 under political pressure following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and returned to the role in 2024 as part of the corporate restructuring that gave the surviving listed entity its current form.

Nebius Group is the Netherlands-domiciled successor to Yandex N.V., reconstituted through a 2024 restructuring that separated the Russian operating business and refocused the surviving parent on AI infrastructure. Alongside the core AI cloud business, the group retains three smaller branded subsidiaries: Toloka AI, which provides human-data labelling for AI training pipelines; TripleTen, an online technology education platform; and Avride, which is developing autonomous driving technology.

## The FY2025 Print

The headline Q4 metrics capture only part of the structural picture. Nebius reported a Q4 net loss of $249.6 million — reflecting the depreciation and stock-compensation weight of a scale-up at speed — but the more consequential line was operating cash flow: $834 million in a single quarter against revenue of $227.7 million. The gap is the customer-prepayment signature. Enterprise AI compute customers, structured like hyperscaler counterparties, prepay for capacity, generating cash ahead of recognised revenue. Nebius was, in the fourth quarter, collecting at nearly four times the rate it was recognising.

Capital expenditure of approximately $2 billion in Q4 alone — a roughly 9x capex-to-revenue ratio — illustrates the build-ahead posture. At year-end, Nebius had 170 megawatts of power actively connected to its data centre footprint, against more than 2 gigawatts under contract. The gap between active and contracted capacity is the physical expression of the investment thesis: the company has secured the grid connections and real estate it believes demand will fill, and is now in the process of filling them.

|---|---|
| Revenue | $227.7M |
| YoY growth (total) | +547% |
| YoY growth (core AI cloud) | +802% |
| Net loss | $249.6M |
| Operating cash flow | $834M |
| Capex (approx.) | ~$2.0B |

## The FY2026 Commitment

Management's guidance for 2026 is, by any peer comparison, the most aggressive public commitment in the AI-cloud sector. [Nebius Q4 2025 earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) puts full-year revenue at $3.0–3.4 billion — implying roughly seven times FY2025 — with an adjusted EBITDA margin target of approximately 40% at the core segment level, capital expenditure of $16–20 billion, and exit ARR of $7–9 billion with more than half of that figure already contracted at the time of guidance. Connected power is targeted at 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt by year-end, a five-to-six-fold physical expansion in a single calendar year.

The contracted-ARR disclosure is the detail that distinguishes guidance from aspiration: Nebius is not projecting $7–9 billion on the basis of pipeline or addressable market; it is stating that the majority of that figure rests on executed customer commitments.

## The Strategic Equity Signal

In August 2025, Nebius closed a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement with three named participants: Accel, Nvidia, and Orbis Investments. The Nvidia component is particularly loaded — Nvidia is simultaneously Nebius's primary GPU supplier and a balance-sheet investor, an alignment of commercial and financial interest that would be difficult to replicate with a competing hardware vendor. Accel's Matt Weigand, a partner since 2013 with a background in enterprise software and security, held observer rights ahead of the August 2025 AGM and was subsequently elected to the board.

## The Central Tension

The question that Nebius's FY2026 commitment poses — and that no equity filing can answer — is whether Volozh's team can convert more than fifty percent of contracted ARR into deployed capacity inside the guidance window. The constraint is not financial: $3.7 billion in cash plus $834 million of Q4 operating cash flow plus the $700 million strategic placement provides the funding base. The constraint is operational: five-to-six-fold power expansion, GPU procurement at scale through a supplier who is also a shareholder, concurrent real estate and utility execution across multiple jurisdictions, and customer ramp management — all while CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Crusoe, and the hyperscalers' own internal AI cloud capacity absorb the same enterprise compute demand Nebius is contracting. The Nvidia strategic alignment offers a procurement advantage that few peers can replicate. Whether that advantage translates into executed megawatts by December 2026 is the question the operating record will settle.

chapters.title: From CompTek to Yandex to Nebius
chapters.body:
## The CompTek seed

The entity that would eventually become Nebius Group N.V. had its earliest origins not in a search algorithm but in a computer-hardware distribution business. In 1990, John Boynton co-founded CompTek International in Moscow — one of the first generation of commercially oriented technology companies to emerge from the collapsing Soviet system. CompTek's role in the subsequent decade was less that of a technology developer than a corporate nursery: it provided the infrastructure, early capital, and operational scaffolding within which Arkady Volozh and his collaborators built and incubated what would become Russia's dominant internet search engine.

Yandex as a named search product launched in 1997, and the company was formally incorporated in 2000. The ownership and board connections forged in the CompTek incubator persisted directly into the incorporated Yandex entity. Boynton joined the Yandex board at inception in 2000 and did not leave it — serving through every phase of the company's subsequent history and assuming the chairmanship in 2016. His tenure represents the longest unbroken thread of institutional memory in what is now the Nebius Group governance structure.

The second foundational financial connection was forged in 1998, when Charles Ryan — then co-founder and chief executive of United Financial Group, one of the leading Russia-focused investment banks of the post-Soviet era — sponsored an early-stage technology investment through ru-Net Holdings that included Yandex. Ryan had previously led the St. Petersburg privatisation programme for the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development; UFG would later be acquired in its entirety by Deutsche Bank, with Ryan serving as Deutsche Bank Group's chief country officer and CEO for Russia from 2005 to 2008. He joined the Yandex board at the 2011 NASDAQ IPO and remained a director through the full arc of the company's subsequent transformation.

## The dominant decade and the 2022 break

Yandex's 2011 NASDAQ IPO raised approximately $1.3 billion and valued the company at roughly $8 billion, at the time one of the largest internet IPOs since Google. The listing reflected a business that by 2011 controlled more than sixty per cent of Russian internet search — a market-share position it held, and in some periods extended, through the following decade. The 2010s saw Yandex diversify aggressively beyond search: ride-hailing through Yandex.Taxi (a joint venture with Uber that eventually became Yandex.Go), food delivery through Yandex.Eats, cloud infrastructure, self-driving technology through Yandex Self-Driving Group, and the broader ecosystem of verticals that characterised the dominant internet platform model of the era. By the early 2020s Yandex was the most complete Russian-language internet ecosystem in existence, with a NASDAQ-listed equity that gave Western institutional capital indirect exposure to Russian consumer internet growth.

Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine ended that proposition. The political and sanctions pressures that followed created an impossible position for a company incorporated in the Netherlands, listed in New York, and operationally headquartered in Moscow. Volozh stepped down as chief executive in June 2022 — a resignation that he later described, in the context of his public distancing from the invasion, as part of a broader personal and corporate reckoning. He remained connected to the ownership and board structure, but the operational leadership of the company changed hands at a moment of acute external pressure.

## Restructuring and rebirth: 2024

The solution that emerged over the following two years was a structural separation of the listed parent from the Russian operating business. In 2024, Yandex N.V. completed what was, in corporate-transaction terms, a substantial divestiture: the entire Russian operating business — the search engine, Yandex.Taxi, the food delivery platforms, the Russian cloud, and the adjacent domestic products — was sold to a consortium of Russian investors. The Netherlands-domiciled parent retained the international assets: the Nvidia GPU-cluster AI cloud business operating in European data centres, Toloka AI (a global human-data labelling platform), TripleTen (an online technology-education business), and Avride (the autonomous driving technology unit, formerly Yandex Self-Driving Group's international operations).

The parent was rebranded Nebius Group N.V. and continued to trade on NASDAQ under the new ticker NBIS. Volozh returned as chief executive to lead the refocused group, combining the institutional credibility of the original founder with the strategic mandate to rebuild the business around AI infrastructure.

The board was reconfigured to match the new strategic identity. Boynton remained as chairman and Ryan as an independent director — the two longest-serving outside directors, whose combined institutional knowledge of the company's founding, IPO, and decade of Russian market dominance gave the post-restructuring entity continuity and credibility with long-term shareholders. Around them, a set of newer directors was assembled to supply the capability set that a Netherlands-domiciled AI infrastructure company required.

## The post-restructuring board build

Ophir Nave joined as chief operating officer in May 2024 and was elected as an executive director at the August 2024 general meeting. His profile was calibrated precisely for the legal-architecture complexity of the restructuring: a Doctor of Juridical Science from Harvard Law School, a clerkship at the Israeli Supreme Court, a period at Wachtell Lipton Rosen & Katz in New York, and a lead partnership in the corporate and M&A practice at Arnon Tadmor-Levy in Israel. The assembly of a Netherlands-incorporated public company retaining international technology assets from a Russian operating entity while maintaining a NASDAQ listing is a feat of cross-border legal engineering; Nave's credential set is the explanation for how it was executed.

Elena Bunina joined as a non-executive director at the same August 2024 meeting. A mathematician with nearly seventy published research papers, she had previously served as general director of human resources and head of academic and educational services across the Yandex Group until April 2022. At Nebius she leads science and education, connecting directly to the TripleTen subsidiary and to the company's longer-term positioning in AI talent development.

Kira Radinsky joined as an independent non-executive director in 2024, bringing the board's most directly AI-domain-aligned credential: chief executive and chairwoman of Diagnostic Robotics, a US-based AI healthcare company, and founder of Mana Bio. Radinsky previously co-founded SalesPredict, an AI-powered sales analytics platform acquired by eBay in 2016, after which she served as eBay's director of data science and chief scientist for Israel. Her addition signalled the governance transformation from a Russia-focused internet conglomerate to an AI-infrastructure company requiring domain-expert oversight.

At the August 2025 annual general meeting, two further directors were elected. Arne Grimme, a partner at De Brauw Blackstone Westbroek and head of its corporate M&A practice, provided the Netherlands-domicile legal anchor the board required: Nebius is an N.V. incorporated under Dutch law, and Grimme's expertise in Dutch corporate governance and cross-border transactions addressed a governance gap. Matthew Weigand, a partner at Accel who had focused on enterprise software, financial technology, and security investments since 2013, joined concurrent with the close of Nebius's $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement — a financing that brought Accel, Nvidia, and Orbis Investments onto the shareholder register. Weigand had held observer rights ahead of his formal election; his board seat formalised the venture-capital governance stake in the AI-infrastructure thesis.

The resulting eight-director board at the snapshot date — Volozh as executive director and CEO, Nave as executive director and COO, Bunina as non-executive director, and five independent non-executive directors in Boynton, Ryan, Radinsky, Grimme, and Weigand — reads as a precise mapping of the strategic transformation: founder continuity plus legal architecture plus AI domain expertise plus Dutch corporate governance plus venture-co-investor oversight, all anchored by the two longest-serving figures who carry the institutional memory from 1990 through to 2026.

## The inflection and what it means

The operating numbers that emerged from the restructured entity by late 2025 established that the corporate transformation had been successfully converted into an AI-infrastructure business with genuine commercial velocity. Q4 2025 revenue reached $227.7 million, a 547 per cent year-on-year increase, with the core AI cloud segment growing at 802 per cent. Exit annual recurring revenue stood at $1.25 billion. The company held $3.7 billion of cash at year-end 2025, with $834 million of operating cash flow generated in Q4 alone — a prepayment signature from enterprise customers that provided working capital ahead of the capital expenditure cycle. Active data centre power reached 170 megawatts against more than 2 gigawatts contracted.

The FY2026 guidance that management issued in February 2026 was the most aggressive public commitment in the AI cloud peer set: revenue of $3.0 to $3.4 billion, capital expenditure of $16 to $20 billion, year-end ARR of $7 to $9 billion with more than half already contracted, and connected power of 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt — a roughly five-fold increase from the year-end 2025 active base.

The thirty-six-year arc from a Moscow hardware-distribution company to a NASDAQ-listed AI cloud operator with a $16 to $20 billion annual capital expenditure programme is, at one level, an improbable straight line. At another, it is a precise illustration of what corporate restructuring can produce when the post-divestiture entity retains the institutional knowledge, the financial resources, and a founder willing to rebuild. The corporate history of Nebius Group is not prologue to the investment thesis — it is the investment thesis. The balance-sheet reconstitution, the board reconfiguration, and the Nvidia strategic relationship that formalised in the $700 million August 2025 placement are all outputs of a restructuring executed with enough speed and legal precision to catch the AI infrastructure cycle before the window narrowed. Whether the FY2026 capacity ramp can be delivered inside the guidance window is the operating question that dominates every subsequent chapter of this analysis; the corporate-history answer is that the organisational capability to attempt it was assembled more rapidly, and from more adverse starting conditions, than any comparable transformation in the current AI-infrastructure cohort.

chapters.title: Core AI cloud plus three branded subsidiaries
chapters.body:
## The Four-Part Architecture

When Nebius Group emerged from the 2024 corporate restructuring that separated Yandex's Russian operating business from the surviving Netherlands holdco, Arkady Volozh inherited not a single asset but a cluster of four distinct businesses, each operating under its own brand, serving different customer bases, and carrying different risk profiles. The largest by revenue and by strategic weight was the core AI cloud — GPU-powered compute infrastructure sold to AI labs, enterprise model developers, and multi-cloud buyers. Around it sat three wholly owned subsidiaries: Toloka AI, a human-data-labelling platform serving the global AI training market; TripleTen, an online tech-education bootcamp targeting data science and software engineering students; and Avride, an autonomous driving research business that sat further from commercial maturity than any of the others. Understanding how those four pieces fit together — and which one was doing the work — was the starting point for any serious analysis of the NBIS equity.

## Core AI Cloud: The Dominant Revenue Engine

The core AI cloud business was, by the time of the Q4 2025 earnings release, the only segment growing fast enough to shape the group's financial trajectory. [Nebius Group Q4 and FY2025 Results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) reported that the core AI cloud segment grew 802% year-over-year in Q4 2025, against a group-level headline of 547% YoY revenue growth to $227.7 million for the quarter. The gap between the segment growth rate and the consolidated rate was, itself, a meaningful piece of information: it indicated that the subsidiary businesses were growing at rates materially below the cloud core, diluting headline growth even as the primary engine accelerated.

The business Nebius was building in that segment was deliberately full-stack. The company procured Nvidia GPU hardware — the H100 and H200 generations that dominated AI training and inference workloads through 2025 — and deployed them inside data centers it designed and operated. The stack did not stop at the hardware layer. Nebius built out the cooling infrastructure, the high-bandwidth networking interconnects, the operating-system-level software, and the developer-facing interfaces that translated physical compute capacity into billable cloud services. Customer access came through two pathways: a self-service platform branded Nebius AI Studio, aimed at AI developers and smaller model-training teams, and direct enterprise contracting for larger, multi-year committed workloads. The enterprise contracting channel was, based on the cash-flow profile, the more consequential one. Q4 operating cash flow of $834 million against Q4 recognised revenue of $227.7 million was the signature of a business collecting prepayments from enterprise customers well in advance of revenue recognition — a pattern consistent with hyperscaler-adjacent multi-year compute contracts rather than spot-market GPU rental.

The geographic footprint at the close of FY2025 was predominantly European. Legacy data center infrastructure in Finland, inherited from the Yandex-era build-out, formed the earliest operational base. US expansion was underway through 2025 and into 2026, though specific US site locations were not separately disclosed in the public filings at the snapshot date. The contracted-power picture told the more precise capacity story: 170 megawatts of active power at year-end 2025, against more than 2,000 megawatts contracted — a ratio of roughly 12-to-1 between pipeline and deployed capacity, representing either an extraordinary forward-commitment book or, depending on execution confidence, the single largest operational risk on the balance sheet.

The Nvidia relationship was the structural variable that distinguished Nebius from most of its peer group. In August 2025, Nebius completed a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement with Accel, Nvidia, and certain accounts of Orbis Investments. [Nebius $700M Strategic Equity Financing](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-announces-oversubscribed-strategic-equity-financing-of-usd-700-million-to-accelerate-roll-out-of-full-stack-ai-infrastructure) Nvidia's participation was dual-role: it was simultaneously the company's primary GPU supplier and a minority equity investor with an aligned financial interest in Nebius's capacity expansion. The implied consequence — that Nebius would receive preferential allocation treatment within Nvidia's constrained GPU output pipeline relative to buyers without equity alignment — was not disclosed as an explicit contractual term but was broadly understood by the investor community as one of the practical benefits of the structure. Specific GPU allocation volumes were not publicly disclosed.

## Toloka AI: The Data-Labelling Complement

Toloka AI operated a crowd-sourced human-data-labelling platform serving AI model developers who needed ground-truth annotation for vision, language, and multimodal training datasets. The business pre-dated the Nebius restructuring, having operated within the Yandex ecosystem as a platform for distributed human intelligence tasks. Under Nebius Group ownership, Toloka was positioned as a complementary revenue line to the core cloud: customers building or fine-tuning AI models frequently needed both compute (which Nebius's cloud provided) and annotated training data (which Toloka supplied). The customer overlap between the two businesses was the strategic logic for keeping them under a single corporate roof rather than spinning Toloka into a standalone entity.

The revenue model was service-based, with hyperscaler-adjacent AI labs and enterprise AI teams among the disclosed customer categories. Toloka competed in a market that included Scale AI, Surge AI, and proprietary internal annotation operations run by the major AI labs themselves. Separate revenue figures for Toloka were not disclosed in the publicly available segment reporting at the snapshot date — the filing basis was consolidated, with the core AI cloud Q4 YoY growth rate of +802% as the cleanest publicly available breakdown.

## TripleTen: The Education Vertical

TripleTen was the most conventionally consumer-facing of the three subsidiaries. The business offered online bootcamp-style courses in data science, software engineering, and AI/ML skills, targeting adult learners seeking career transitions or upskilling in technology disciplines. It operated with its own management team and brand identity, sitting within the Nebius Group consolidated perimeter but functionally independent.

The strategic rationale for retaining TripleTen within the group was less obvious than for Toloka. Tech education was a market with its own competitive dynamics — dominated by platforms such as Coursera, Udemy, and direct university extension programs — and the revenue profile was unlikely to scale proportionally to the AI cloud core. Group management had not publicly indicated plans to separate TripleTen as of the snapshot date, and the business continued to consolidate into group financials without separate revenue disclosure.

## Avride: The Long-Cycle Moonshot

Avride was the business furthest from near-term commercial relevance but carrying the longest potential upside horizon. The autonomous driving and robotics platform was characterised in the group's investor communications as a long-cycle R&D holding — the closest peer analogies were Waymo (Alphabet subsidiary), Aurora Innovation, or the earlier-stage development phase of Cruise (General Motors). Like those peers, Avride consumed capital in pursuit of technical milestones that would precede any commercial deployment at scale. It contributed no material revenue to the FY2025 consolidated results.

The group's retention of Avride reflected, in part, the talent and intellectual-property base that had survived the restructuring from Yandex. Yandex had operated a self-driving research program, SDG, that was among the more sophisticated autonomous-vehicle efforts outside the United States and China during its active phase. What Avride inherited of that program's personnel and technology remained a disclosed but detail-sparse element of the group's asset base. Avride's path to monetisation — licensing, strategic partnership, or independent market entry — was unresolved within the snapshot window.

## Revenue Mix and Disclosure Constraints

The segment architecture was clear at the product-brand level. The revenue arithmetic within it was not. Nebius did not separately disclose product-line revenue for Toloka, TripleTen, or Avride in the publicly summarised FY2025 filings or the Q4 earnings release. The disclosable figure that most closely captured the core AI cloud contribution was the +802% Q4 YoY growth rate — a rate that implied the core segment's absolute revenue substantially dominated the consolidated $227.7 million Q4 print, with the three subsidiaries contributing the residual. Analysts and investors modelling the business were working from that implied split rather than stated segment financials.

| Metric | Q4 2025 | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Group revenue | $227.7M | $3.0–3.4B |
| Core AI cloud YoY growth | +802% | Not separately guided |
| Annualised run rate (ARR) | $1.25B exit-2025 | $7–9B |
| ARR contracted share | — | >50% |
| Active power | 170MW | 800–1,000MW |
| Capex | ~$2B (Q4 only) | $16–20B |

[Source: Nebius Group Q4 and FY2025 Results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results)

## Structural Position: The Advantages and the Asymmetric Risk

The balance-sheet endowment that Nebius carried into FY2026 was genuinely unusual in its competitive set. $3.7 billion of cash at year-end 2025, augmented by the $834 million Q4 operating cash flow, gave the group a funding runway for the $16–20 billion FY2026 capex programme that no pure-play AI cloud competitor without direct balance-sheet backing could replicate unassisted. CoreWeave, the most comparable public peer, had accessed debt markets at scale to fund its build; Nebius entered FY2026 with equity capital already in place and contracted ARR covering more than half of the $7–9 billion target.

The structural disadvantage was the starting position. Nebius was ramping from a post-restructuring base, not from a multi-year operating history as an independent AI cloud company. The 170 megawatts of active power against 2,000-plus megawatts contracted was a gap that required simultaneous execution across power utility agreements, real estate site development, Nvidia GPU delivery schedules, mechanical and electrical construction, and customer onboarding — in multiple geographies, in a single fiscal year. That execution complexity, rather than any question of demand or funding, was the primary risk the group's FY2026 guidance embedded.

chapters.title: $3.7B cash and the $20B capex bar
chapters.body:
## The FY2025 Inflection

When Nebius published its fourth-quarter 2025 results on 12 February 2026, the numbers removed any remaining ambiguity about the company's ambitions. [Q4 revenue came in at $227.7 million, up 547 percent year-on-year](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results). The core AI cloud segment grew 802 percent. The company exited the year with an annualised revenue run rate of $1.25 billion and $3.7 billion of cash on the balance sheet. In the final quarter alone, Nebius deployed approximately $2 billion of capital expenditure. Active connected power reached 170 megawatts against more than 2 gigawatts of contracted future capacity.

The quarter's revenue figure came in below consensus expectations of roughly $247 million. That miss mattered less than the direction of travel. Guidance for FY2026 — revenue of $3 to $3.4 billion, capital expenditure of $16 to $20 billion, ARR of $7 to $9 billion with more than half already contracted — was the most aggressive full-year commitment any publicly listed AI cloud company had issued. The equity market's reaction was to price the guidance, not the miss.

## The Prepayment Signature

The most structurally important disclosure in the Q4 print was not on the income statement. [Operating cash flow for the quarter totalled $834 million against reported revenue of $227.7 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm) — a ratio of approximately 3.7 times.

That gap is the fingerprint of hyperscaler-style customer prepayment. Enterprise and research customers paying for future GPU compute capacity in advance generate cash immediately; that cash is recorded as deferred revenue and recognised only when capacity is consumed. The dynamic is structurally familiar from AWS and Azure reserved-instance arrangements and from CoreWeave's disclosed prepayment terms. At Nebius, the Q4 ratio — cash collected running at 3.7 times revenue recognised — indicated that a substantial book of forward commitments had been signed and partially funded heading into 2026.

The implication for the FY2026 guidance was direct. When management described more than 50 percent of the $7 to $9 billion ARR target as already contracted at guidance issuance, they were not projecting from pipeline probability. They were projecting from signed agreements with cash-deposit mechanics already in motion. The operating cash flow dynamics offered partial corroboration that characterisation was accurate at year-end 2025.

## Walking the Guidance Arithmetic

The FY2026 guidance represented one of the most concentrated tables of forward financial commitments in the AI-infrastructure sector.

| Metric | FY2025 Reference | FY2026 Guidance | Implied Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $227.7M (Q4 run-rate) | $3.0–$3.4B | ~7× FY25 |
| ARR (exit) | $1.25B | $7–$9B | 5.6–7.2× |
| Capex | ~$2B (Q4 alone) | $16–$20B | — |
| Connected power | 170 MW | 800 MW–1 GW | 4.7–5.9× |
| Adj. EBITDA margin | 24% (Q4 2025) | ~40% | +16 pp |
| Contracted ARR share | — | >50% | — |

[Source: Nebius Q4 2025 6-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm)

The revenue guidance of $3 to $3.4 billion implied approximately seven times FY2025 revenue at the midpoint. That growth rate was not plausibly modelled as speculative pipeline in February 2026; it required the contracted-ARR coverage already embedded in the signed book to convert into delivered capacity and recognised revenue on schedule across the year.

The ARR target of $7 to $9 billion is a forward-looking exit figure — the run rate the company intended to reach by 31 December 2026. Working backward: if exit ARR reaches the $8 billion midpoint, Q4 2026 revenue would approach $2 billion in a single quarter — seventeen times the Q4 2024 base. Management commentary in the [earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) indicated more than half of that range was contracted at issuance, providing a structural floor beneath the headline figures rather than a speculative ceiling.

## The Capex Arithmetic

The most challenging line in the guidance was capital expenditure: $16 to $20 billion for FY2026 against projected revenue of $3 to $3.4 billion. That is a capex-to-revenue ratio of between 4.7 and 6.7 times — a ratio with no parallel in the history of publicly listed AI cloud infrastructure at this revenue baseline.

Nebius was not building incrementally against existing utilisation. It was constructing capacity ahead of demand — acquiring and fitting out data centre facilities, executing GPU procurement with Nvidia, and activating power utility agreements, all simultaneously. In Q4 2025 alone, approximately $2 billion of capital expenditure was deployed against $227.7 million of revenue: a 9-times single-quarter ratio. The FY2026 guidance implied this pace would not only continue but accelerate. On a straight-line basis, $16 to $20 billion over four quarters averages $4 to $5 billion per quarter — a doubling to two-and-a-half times the Q4 2025 quarterly rate.

The build-ahead-of-demand model is structurally sound only if contracted ARR converts. Infrastructure purchased to fulfil commitments that slip or cancel becomes stranded depreciation. The fact that customer prepayments were already generating $834 million of operating cash flow in a single quarter against $227.7 million of recognised revenue was, in the Q4 print, the single most important signal that contract quality was sufficient to justify the commitment pace.

## The Financing Stack

At year-end 2025, Nebius held $3.7 billion in cash and liquid equivalents. That figure reflected the accumulation of the August 2025 $700 million strategic equity placement — conducted at an oversubscribed close — alongside the conversion of contracted ARR into advance-payment receipts through the year.

The participants in the August 2025 placement were publicly disclosed as Accel, Nvidia, and certain accounts managed by Orbis Investments. Accel's Matt Weigand received observer rights at the transaction close and was subsequently elected to the board at the August 2025 annual general meeting. Nvidia's participation formalised what had previously been an implied supply relationship: as the dominant GPU vendor to the AI cloud sector, Nvidia's equity stake in Nebius aligned the interests of infrastructure customer and hardware supplier in a way that carried structural implications for allocation priority during periods of constrained supply.

Against a capex guidance of $16 to $20 billion, the $3.7 billion year-end cash position covered between 18 and 23 percent of the low-to-high range. Management guidance acknowledged explicitly that the capex programme exceeded cash on hand and that additional financing — through customer prepayments, potential debt issuance, or further equity — would be required during the year. The operating cash flow dynamics suggested customer prepayments were already partially absorbing this gap, but the magnitude of the buildout required at least one additional capital-markets transaction within the guidance window to fund full execution.

The strategic-investor structure of the August 2025 placement reframed the equity story at a critical moment. Coming within months of the company's operational re-listing on NASDAQ as Nebius Group, an oversubscribed close with named institutional and corporate participants — one of them the world's most valuable semiconductor company — provided a de facto validation certificate from the infrastructure investment community precisely when market credibility was most consequential.

## The Margin Mechanics

The adjusted EBITDA margin trajectory deserves separate treatment because it is the mechanism through which the operating model becomes self-reinforcing at scale.

Nebius reported adjusted EBITDA margin on its core AI cloud segment of 19 percent in Q3 2025. In Q4 2025, [that figure expanded to 24 percent](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm) — a 5 percentage point sequential expansion in one quarter as fixed operating costs began to distribute across a faster-growing revenue base. The FY2026 guidance targeted approximately 40 percent adjusted EBITDA margin — 16 percentage points above the Q4 2025 exit rate. Reaching 40 percent requires that revenue growth materially outpaces incremental operating expenditure in areas like headcount, customer support, and network operations, while the buildout spend is captured in capex and depreciation below the adjusted EBITDA line.

The Q4 net loss of $249.6 million illustrates why the GAAP income statement is a lagging and partial indicator of operating health at this stage of the ramp. A significant portion of that loss reflects depreciation on infrastructure deployed ahead of the revenue curve and non-cash stock-based compensation associated with the management team reconstituted after the 2024 restructuring. The $834 million operating cash flow figure, by contrast, reflected the business's actual cash-generation capacity in a quarter when customer commitments were converting to advance payments faster than infrastructure could be recognised as revenue — a divergence that understates economic progress on the GAAP income statement and overstates it on nothing at all; it simply reflects the timing architecture of the prepayment model.

## The Power Problem — and What It Signals

The connected power trajectory is, in some respects, the most legible proxy for execution progress available to external observers. Software and contractual commitments are difficult to audit from SEC filings; megawatts of activated data centre power are not.

Nebius reported 170 megawatts of active connected power at year-end 2025 against more than 2 gigawatts contracted across its facility portfolio. The FY2026 guidance called for 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt of active connected power by year-end 2026 — a 4.7-fold to 5.9-fold expansion in activated physical capacity in twelve months, a rate with few precedents outside hyperscaler construction programmes operating at dramatically larger absolute scale.

The 2-gigawatt contracted figure provided a ceiling: Nebius had secured the utility agreements and site commitments to support the guidance target in principle. The execution question was whether activation of that contracted capacity could be paced to match Nvidia GPU delivery schedules and customer deployment timelines. In an environment where GPU allocations remained a binding constraint for AI infrastructure capacity, the August 2025 equity investment by Nvidia was directly relevant: a supplier with a financial stake in the customer's growth carries a material incentive to prioritise that customer's allocation requests.

At 170 megawatts active against 2 gigawatts contracted, Nebius ended 2025 with roughly 8.5 percent of its contracted capacity producing revenue. The gap between that figure and the 40-percent-plus EBITDA margin target for 2026 describes the entire financial story the numbers were telling — a company that had secured commitments far in excess of its current operating footprint, had begun to activate that footprint at pace, and was committing $3.7 billion of cash plus the most aggressive public guidance in the sector to the proposition that the activation curve would prove as steep as the revenue and ARR projections required.

chapters.title: From restructuring print to first-billion ARR
chapters.body:
## The opening prints: out of the restructuring window

When Nebius Group disclosed its earliest post-restructuring quarterly results through 2025, the numbers were, by design, modest. The company that emerged from Yandex N.V.'s 2024 corporate separation was not a going concern with a seasoned customer base and a stable revenue line — it was a Netherlands-domiciled holding company with a GPU-cluster footprint in European data centres, roughly $3.7 billion of cash from the restructuring settlement, and a thesis about what AI infrastructure demand would look like at scale.

The early 2025 quarters told a familiar build-ahead story. Revenue scaled from a small base as the company signed its initial cohort of enterprise AI customers, provisioned capacity in European data centres, and began the laborious work of converting contracted commitments into recognised revenue under IFRS. Management communicated the ramp in terms that investors in hyperscaler capex cycles would recognise: the upfront investment thesis, the long-lead-time nature of GPU procurement, and the customer prepayment dynamic that would eventually become the most structurally distinctive feature of Nebius's reported financials.

What distinguished Nebius from the broader AI-cloud cohort in this period was not the pace of early revenue — it was the scale of the infrastructure commitment being built ahead of it.

## August 2025: the capital event that reset the investment narrative

The most consequential single capital-markets event of Nebius's post-restructuring life arrived in August 2025, when the company closed a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement from Accel, Nvidia, and certain accounts managed by Orbis Investments. [Source: Nebius Group IR, group.nebius.com]

The placement's oversubscription was itself a signal, but it was the Nvidia participation that carried the most structural weight. Nvidia was simultaneously Nebius's dominant GPU supplier and, from August 2025 forward, a strategic equity investor. That alignment created a form of circular reinforcement that investors in the AI-infrastructure cycle had learned to parse carefully: an equity stake gives Nvidia a financial interest in Nebius's capacity ramp succeeding, which in turn shapes GPU allocation priority — a scarce resource that had become as strategically important as any clause in an enterprise cloud contract.

Accel's participation arrived with governance consequences. The firm's Matt Weigand received observer rights concurrent with the investment, and at the August 2025 annual general meeting, Weigand and Arne Grimme — a De Brauw Blackstone Westbroek corporate M&A partner — were elected to the board as independent non-executive directors. The additions completed a governance architecture that combined Yandex-legacy institutional memory with oversight capabilities appropriate to a NASDAQ-listed AI infrastructure company executing what would become a $16–20 billion multi-year capex programme.

The $700 million placement funded the Q3–Q4 2025 infrastructure ramp that produced the numbers on which Nebius's investment case would ultimately rest.

## Q3 2025: the trajectory clarifies

By the third quarter of 2025, the shape of the ramp had become legible to investors tracking the company's disclosures. Annualised recurring revenue had approached approximately $700 million — a figure that, while still sub-scale relative to the guidance management would eventually set for FY2026, represented a meaningful acceleration from the early-year base. [Source: Nebius 6-K, SEC EDGAR]

The core AI cloud segment was growing faster than the consolidated entity, as Nebius's portfolio subsidiaries — Toloka AI's human-data labelling business, TripleTen's online tech-education platform, and Avride's autonomous-driving unit — contributed revenue at materially lower growth rates. The margin trajectory was also improving: the adjusted EBITDA margin for the core segment reached 19% in Q3, a data point that management would later reference in the context of the FY2026 margin target.

The Q3 print established a pattern that would define the equity's trading behaviour through the back half of 2025: each quarterly disclosure was read not for its absolute revenue number — still modest relative to peer-set benchmarks — but for the acceleration implied in the ARR trajectory and the physical capacity being brought online behind it.

## February 12, 2026: the earnings release as inflection event

The Q4 2025 and full-year results, released on February 12, 2026, reframed the entire preceding year as prologue.

Consolidated quarterly revenue came in at $227.7 million, representing 547% year-on-year growth. [Source: Nebius Group, Business Wire, February 12 2026](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) The core AI cloud segment, isolated from portfolio subsidiaries, posted 802% year-on-year growth in the quarter. The exit ARR reached $1.25 billion, up from the approximate $700 million annualised run-rate of Q3.

The headline revenue figure was, on its own terms, a miss. Analyst consensus had stood at roughly $247 million; the reported $227.7 million fell short by approximately 8%. In practice, however, the market's reaction to that gap was subordinated to what management disclosed alongside it.

The Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin for the core segment reached 24%, up five percentage points from Q3's 19% exit. Operating cash flow in the quarter was $834 million against $227.7 million of revenue. The divergence — nearly four dollars of operating cash inflow for every dollar of recognised revenue — was the clearest expression of the customer prepayment dynamic Nebius had described throughout 2025. Enterprise AI customers booking large compute contracts prepay for capacity; the cash arrives before the associated revenue is recognised under IFRS conventions. The $834 million Q4 operating cash flow was not a trading profit — it was the advance-payment signature of a business whose customers were committing to capacity months before they would consume it.

Year-end cash stood at $3.7 billion. [Source: Nebius 20-F, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925015480/tm257185d1_ex99-1.htm) Capex in Q4 alone approximated $2 billion — a 9x capex-to-revenue ratio reflecting the build-ahead-of-demand posture of a company acquiring AI processor inventory and data centre power well before the contracted revenue associated with that capacity had begun to flow through the income statement.

Active connected power at year-end was 170 megawatts, against more than 2 gigawatts of contracted power — a 12:1 ratio of contracted-to-active capacity that expressed both the scale of the FY2026 execution challenge and the forward-demand visibility that management was translating into guidance.

## The FY2026 guidance: the most aggressive public commitment in the peer set

The targets management set for FY2026 on February 12 placed Nebius in a category of its own among publicly listed AI-cloud peers.

| Metric | FY2025 (Q4 / Exit) | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Quarterly revenue | $227.7M (+547% YoY) | — |
| Full-year revenue | — | $3.0–3.4B |
| Adj. EBITDA margin (core) | 24% (Q4 exit) | ~40% |
| Year-end ARR | $1.25B | $7–9B |
| Capex | ~$2B in Q4 alone | $16–20B |
| Connected power (active) | 170MW | 800MW–1GW |

Revenue guidance of $3.0 to $3.4 billion implied roughly seven-fold growth over full-year 2025. The adjusted EBITDA margin target of approximately 40% — against the 24% Q4 exit rate — implied a substantial operating-leverage inflection as fixed infrastructure costs were spread across a materially higher revenue base, with depreciation curves bending as previously capitalised assets entered productive service.

The ARR target of $7 to $9 billion, with more than half of that amount already contracted at the time of the guidance disclosure, provided a degree of demand-side visibility unusual in AI-cloud forward guidance. Contracted ARR is not recognised revenue — it is signed customer commitments, subject to delivery — but the greater-than-50% contracted share translated the FY2026 ARR range from a speculative pipeline estimate into something closer to an execution question: could Nebius deploy the capacity fast enough to satisfy commitments already on paper?

The physical dimension of the guidance was its most ambitious component. Scaling connected power from 170 megawatts at year-end 2025 to 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt at year-end 2026 required concurrent execution across power utility agreements, real-estate procurement, hardware supply — contingent on Nvidia GPU allocation — and customer onboarding at a pace without clear precedent among public AI-cloud issuers. The capex envelope of $16 to $20 billion, against starting cash of $3.7 billion, presupposed significant additional financing, with the customer-prepayment cash dynamics serving as one structural bridge and the Nvidia strategic relationship providing the supply-chain alignment that made the physical ramp plausible.

## Seven quarters in: a compression without precedent in the peer set

Taken across the seven public quarters since the Nebius brand and strategy were established, the cumulative narrative is one of unusual compression. The company executed a corporate restructuring — separating a Russia-domiciled operating business from a Netherlands holding company and relisting on NASDAQ under a new ticker — while simultaneously rebuilding a balance sheet from settlement cash, constructing an AI-cloud infrastructure footprint, recruiting a customer base capable of generating $1.25 billion in ARR, and closing the most strategically consequential equity financing of its short public history.

The 547% Q4 revenue growth figure, striking in isolation, understated the transformation when viewed against the restructuring baseline. Nebius did not accelerate an existing AI-cloud business — it built one inside a restructured holding company while that company was simultaneously resolving its post-Yandex governance architecture and assembling the capital stack required to fund a $16–20 billion infrastructure programme.

The February 12, 2026 earnings release was the moment the sum of those parts became legible as a single coherent story: a corporate reorganisation that had, inside seven public quarters, become one of the most aggressive AI-infrastructure-capacity expansion narratives in the public-equity cycle.

chapters.title: Yandex legacy plus the Accel-and-Nvidia-aligned new arrivals
chapters.body:
## The Founder Returns

When Arkady Volozh walked back through the door at Yandex's successor entity in 2024, he carried something no hire could replicate: he had built the original company from a CompTek incubator project into one of Europe's most sophisticated technology organisations, led it through a 2011 NASDAQ listing that valued it at more than $8 billion, and shepherded the international asset base through the most turbulent period in Russian corporate history. His 2022 departure — made in the context of post-invasion political pressure, with Volozh publicly condemning the war in Ukraine — had been framed by observers as an act of severance from the Russian state machinery his company had become entangled with. His return in 2024, as founder and CEO of a fundamentally different entity, reframed that departure as prelude rather than epilogue.

The corporate structure Volozh returned to lead was itself a product of controlled demolition and reconstruction. Nebius Group N.V., the Netherlands-domiciled holding company that retained Yandex's international assets after the sale of the Russian operating business, was effectively a blank-slate vehicle carrying one critical asset: a balance sheet that, by the end of 2025, held $3.7 billion in cash and had generated $834 million in operating cash flow in Q4 alone. That financial foundation, combined with Volozh's institutional credibility as the original architect of what Yandex had been, allowed the company to recruit capital at a scale that validated the AI-infrastructure thesis: a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement from Accel, Nvidia, and Orbis in August 2025.

The board Volozh led into that financing was itself the product of deliberate construction — three figures who carried the institutional memory of the old Yandex, paired with five newer arrivals whose individual profiles mapped precisely onto the challenges a Netherlands-domiciled, NASDAQ-listed AI infrastructure company needed to solve.

## The Institutional Memory Layer

John Boynton had been in the room before Yandex was Yandex. In 1990, he co-founded CompTek International, the company that incubated Yandex itself, and has sat on the Yandex and Nebius board continuously since 2000. He became chairman in 2016, meaning he held the chair through the 2022 invasion, the board decisions around Volozh's departure, the prolonged and technically complex negotiation to separate the Russian operating assets, and the 2024 restructuring that produced Nebius Group. That unbroken continuity across what were effectively three different versions of the same public company — Russian-market Yandex, dual-listing Yandex, and AI-infrastructure Nebius — represents a quality of institutional knowledge that no external appointment could have substituted.

Outside his Nebius role, Boynton remained active in early-stage technology through Firehouse Capital, his private investment vehicle, and had recently co-founded Litix, a vertical SaaS AI company targeting public-sector organisations. The Litix co-founding was a material contemporary signal: the chairman of a company pursuing an aggressive AI infrastructure thesis was himself, in a separate capacity, building an AI application business on top of infrastructure like the kind Nebius was deploying.

Charles Ryan's connection to Yandex was longer by one originating act. In 1998, while co-running United Financial Group, the Russia-focused investment bank he had co-founded in 1994, Ryan initiated a New Technology Group within UFG and sponsored the early-stage investment in ru-Net Holdings — the vehicle that included Yandex. That original financial sponsorship preceded the 2011 NASDAQ IPO by thirteen years; Ryan joined the board at the IPO and remained through the full cycle. His career had traced the arc of Western financial engagement with Russia: CS First Boston analyst in 1989, then the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in London from 1991 to 1994, where he led the St. Petersburg privatisation program, then UFG, then Chief Country Officer and CEO of Deutsche Bank Group in Russia from 2005 to 2008, after Deutsche Bank's acquisition of UFG's investment banking business.

Ryan's contemporary role as General Partner at Almaz Capital Partners — a Silicon Valley venture firm explicitly positioned around US-Eastern Europe technology connections — made him something more than a legacy director. He was an active conduit for the engineering-talent and deal-flow networks that had always underpinned Yandex's technical edge and that Nebius was attempting to reconstitute in a different geography.

## The Legal Architecture

The person most responsible for the technical construction of the entity that Volozh, Boynton, and Ryan were now governing was Ophir Nave, who joined as Chief Operating Officer in May 2024 and was elected Executive Director at the August 2024 annual general meeting. Nave's credentials were almost comically well-matched to the task: a Doctor of Juridical Science from Harvard Law School, an LL.B. from Tel Aviv University, a stint clerking for the Israeli Supreme Court, a career as Lead Partner in the Corporate and M&A practice at Arnon Tadmor-Levy in Israel, and previous time at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz in New York — the firm whose M&A and transactional pedigree is among the most selective in the American legal market. Nave had also lectured on corporate finance at Tel Aviv University.

Separating a multi-billion-dollar Russian operating business from a Netherlands public limited company listed on NASDAQ, while preserving the listing status, managing the shareholder base, and positioning the surviving entity for a new strategic direction, was precisely the category of transaction that a Harvard SJD combined with Wachtell M&A training was built for. The board composition formalised what had already been an operational reality: Nave ran the architecture of the transaction, and his elevation to Executive Director recognised that the post-restructuring corporate form itself was his primary deliverable.

## The Science and Education Thread

Elena Bunina joined the board as Non-Executive Director in August 2024, simultaneously in her operational role as Head of Science and Education. An Israel-based mathematician with close to seventy research publications, she had previously served as Head of Academic and Educational Services across the Yandex Group and, until April 2022, as both General Director and Director of Human Resources at Yandex LLC — the Russian operating entity. Her departure from those roles in April 2022 placed her in the same temporal frame as Volozh's own exit from day-to-day operations.

Bunina's Nebius role connected directly to TripleTen, the online tech-education subsidiary that sat within the group's portfolio alongside Toloka AI (human-data labelling) and Avride (autonomous driving). For an AI infrastructure company whose long-term competitive position depended partly on the supply of technical labour capable of operating GPU clusters and building on top of them, having a director and operational head with deep roots in technology education and a publishing record in mathematics was not merely institutional continuity — it was a credential that spoke to the pipeline.

## The AI-Domain and Governance Additions

Kira Radinsky joined as an Independent Non-Executive Director in 2024, representing the most directly AI-native profile on the board. As CEO and Chairwoman of Diagnostic Robotics, a US-based company applying AI to healthcare systems, and as founder of Mana Bio, an AI-based drug-delivery venture, her operational experience was in building and leading AI application businesses at scale. The prior history was also instructive: Radinsky co-founded SalesPredict, an AI-driven sales-prediction company, which eBay acquired in 2016; she subsequently served as Director of Data Science and IL Chief Scientist at eBay following the acquisition. That trajectory — AI startup founder, successful exit, integration into a large technology company, then back to founding — was the pattern of a practitioner, not a credentialist.

For a board that needed to evaluate AI infrastructure investment decisions that would eventually be measured against the performance of AI application customers, having a director who had been on both sides of that infrastructure-application divide carried specific utility.

The August 2025 AGM brought two further additions who, taken together, represented the governance consequences of the $700 million financing completed that same month.

Arne Grimme, who had been a partner at De Brauw Blackstone Westbroek — the leading Dutch corporate law firm — since 2003 and led its Corporate M&A practice, joined as Independent Non-Executive Director. Nebius Group N.V. was a Netherlands public limited company, and the post-restructuring corporate form was structured under Dutch law. Grimme's appointment was the formal anchoring of Netherlands-domicile governance expertise into the boardroom itself: not external counsel engaged on a transaction, but a resident expert in the corporate structures governing the entity.

Matthew Weigand, a Partner at Accel since 2013 with a focus on enterprise software, financial technology, and security businesses, joined the board at the same AGM. Accel had been one of the three strategic participants in the $700 million equity placement, alongside Nvidia and Orbis. Weigand had held observer rights prior to his formal election. His pre-Accel career had been in technology investment banking at William Blair.

The significance of Weigand's appointment extended beyond the governance mechanics of a co-investor gaining board representation. Accel's participation in the $700 million placement — an oversubscribed round, according to Nebius's investor communications — alongside Nvidia was a statement about the perceived credibility of the AI infrastructure thesis. Nvidia's interest in Nebius as a strategic customer and equity investee required no translation: a company buying GPU clusters at the scale Nebius projected for FY2026 (capex guidance of $16 to $20 billion, with connected power targeted at 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt by year-end) was a strategic counterparty for Nvidia regardless of equity. Accel's participation was the independent venture validation — a firm with no hardware supply interest was making the same bet.

## The Board as Strategic Blueprint

Viewed as a whole, the eight-director composition was a legible document.

| Director | Role | Primary Credential for Nebius |
|---|---|---|
| Arkady Volozh | CEO, Executive Director | Founder; institutional credibility; AI-infra thesis originator |
| John Boynton | Independent Non-Executive Chairman | CompTek co-founder; board since 2000; unbroken continuity |
| Charles E. Ryan | Independent Non-Executive Director | Russia-finance bridge; Almaz Capital GP; 2011 IPO continuity |
| Ophir Nave | COO, Executive Director | Harvard SJD + Wachtell M&A; post-restructuring legal architect |
| Elena Bunina | Head of Science & Education, Non-Executive Director | Mathematician; 70 publications; TripleTen/education pipeline |
| Kira Radinsky | Independent Non-Executive Director | Diagnostic Robotics CEO; AI-application domain expertise |
| Arne Grimme | Independent Non-Executive Director | De Brauw partner; Dutch corporate M&A; Netherlands-domicile anchor |
| Matthew Weigand | Independent Non-Executive Director | Accel partner; $700M placement co-investor; enterprise software VC |

The three Yandex-legacy figures — Boynton, Ryan, and Volozh — supplied the institutional memory and the credibility required to maintain a NASDAQ listing through an exceptional period of corporate transformation. None of the five newer arrivals were legacy appointments: each mapped onto a specific technical or strategic requirement of the company Nebius was becoming. Nave built the legal form. Bunina managed the talent and education pipeline. Radinsky provided AI-domain pattern recognition. Grimme embedded Dutch corporate law expertise. Weigand brought the venture governance and the co-investor alignment signal.

The Accel and Nvidia placement, consummated in August 2025, was the event that crystallised the narrative. A company running $1.25 billion in annualised recurring revenue at year-end 2025 and targeting $7 to $9 billion in ARR by the end of 2026 — with more than half of that contracted — required more than a capable CEO and a strong balance sheet. It required a board whose composition could independently validate each component of that thesis to the institutional investors being asked to fund it. The structure Volozh assembled, layer by Yandex veteran and new arrival, was that validation made organisational.

chapters.title: Hyperscaler-adjacent customers, Nvidia-aligned supply
chapters.body:
## Who Was Buying — and Why That Mattered

Nebius did not publish a customer list. That was not an oversight. It was characteristic of the segment it had chosen to serve.

The enterprise AI infrastructure market operates through multi-year framework agreements signed under non-disclosure, a contracting culture imported from the hyperscalers whose overflow Nebius was explicitly designed to absorb. The company described its customer base in structural terms rather than by name: AI laboratories and foundation-model developers consuming GPU compute for training runs; multi-cloud enterprise buyers who required burst capacity outside a primary hyperscaler relationship; and production inference customers deploying at scale and seeking guaranteed resource availability. What Nebius's disclosure did confirm — in the [February 2026 Q4 earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) — was that more than half of its $7–9 billion FY2026 annual recurring revenue target was already contracted by the time those results were published. That single data point defined the company's revenue quality in a way that customer names could not.

The distinction between contracted ARR and spot-market GPU cloud revenue was not cosmetic. Spot AI cloud markets — the GPU rental services that priced H100 access by the hour — carried structural churn risk tied to model-training cycle lengths, lab funding cycles, and capacity overhang from incumbent hyperscalers. Multi-year commercial commitments from enterprise buyers of Nebius's scale meant credit-worthy counterparties had signed binding purchase obligations, providing revenue visibility of a kind more common to enterprise software than to cloud-infrastructure businesses at an equivalent growth rate. The $834 million in operating cash flow Nebius generated in Q4 2025 alone — against $227.7 million in revenue — reflected that contracting structure directly: customer prepayments accruing well ahead of recognised revenue, a balance-sheet signature associated with hyperscaler-style commercial terms rather than spot-market rentals.

## The Nvidia Equation

No single relationship on Nebius's counterparty map carried as much strategic weight as the one with Nvidia.

In August 2025, Nebius closed a $700 million [oversubscribed strategic equity placement](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-announces-oversubscribed-strategic-equity-financing-of-usd-700-million-to-accelerate-roll-out-of-full-stack-ai-infrastructure), with Nvidia participating alongside Accel and Orbis Investments. The placement was not a passive financial investment. Nvidia's decision to take an equity stake in an AI cloud company — at a moment when it was simultaneously the dominant supplier of the compute those clouds required — created a category of alignment that constrained how to think about Nebius's GPU supply position. The company did not publicly disclose specific allocation terms or volumes. What it did make visible was the broader logic: a GPU supplier that held equity in a customer had interests that diverged sharply from a purely transactional supplier-customer relationship.

Nvidia's GPU roadmap, running through the H100 and H200 generations to the B100 and B200 Blackwell architecture and into the Rubin platform, was the backbone of every serious AI cloud business's capacity plan in 2025. The allocation question — who received priority in a supply-constrained environment — was the defining competitive variable for independent AI cloud operators. CoreWeave, the closest comparable public company at the time, had established its Nvidia relationship through years of early-adopter purchasing and had similarly positioned that alignment as a structural advantage. Nebius's $700 million placement inserted Nvidia as a financial co-owner at a moment when Nebius was simultaneously planning the most aggressive capital expenditure program any AI-cloud company had publicly committed to: $16–20 billion in capex across FY2026.

The implied logic was circular in the best sense. Nvidia's equity stake gave it a financial incentive to see Nebius's capacity ramp succeed. Nebius's capacity ramp required GPU allocations at scale. A supplier whose equity value increased with a customer's growth had structurally different behaviour than one negotiating at arm's length. None of that was guaranteed. Specific allocation commitments were not in the public record. But the geometry of the relationship was visible enough that the August 2025 placement was, in effect, a public signal from Nvidia about which independent AI cloud operators it considered strategically important.

## Power as the Binding Constraint

If GPU allocation was the most consequential uncertainty, power was the slowest-moving constraint.

Nebius exited 2025 with 170 megawatts of connected power against more than 2,000 megawatts under contract. That 12-to-1 gap between contracted and active power capacity was not a sign of idle strategy — it was a map of the construction pipeline. Power utility agreements, site acquisitions, grid interconnections, cooling infrastructure, and data centre build-out each carried their own lead times, regulatory dependencies, and execution risk. Nebius's FY2026 target of 800–1,000 megawatts of connected power represented a five- to six-fold physical expansion in a single year. The company's European footprint — centred on Finland, where the legacy Yandex data centre infrastructure provided a starting base — was being supplemented by US site development as the company pursued geographic diversification of its capacity.

The practical execution sequence was constrained by physics rather than capital. Money could accelerate site acquisition and vendor commitments. It could not compress utility interconnection timelines or the lead times on large-format cooling deployments. The $2 billion in capital expenditure Nebius deployed in Q4 2025 alone — a 9-to-1 capex-to-revenue ratio for that quarter — demonstrated the company's willingness to spend ahead of revenue. Whether the physical infrastructure could commission fast enough to meet the contracted customer obligations was the operational question that the FY2026 guidance window would answer.

The hardware supply chain sitting between GPU procurement and operational data centre capacity was not separately disclosed at the vendor level. Based on publicly available information about comparable AI infrastructure deployments, the likely server and networking vendors included Supermicro, Dell, HPE, and contract manufacturers including Foxconn-FII and direct ODM suppliers building to Nebius's specifications. These were not differentiated relationships — they were the standard supply chain for any company purchasing Nvidia GPU clusters at scale. The differentiation resided upstream, in the Nvidia relationship itself, and downstream, in the contracted customer base.

## The Investor Constellation

The three co-investors in the August 2025 placement read as a deliberate construction of the capital-structure argument.

Accel, the tier-one venture capital firm, brought enterprise software credibility and an AI-infrastructure portfolio that complemented Nebius's strategic positioning. The placement brought Accel partner Matthew Weigand onto the Nebius board — an observer seat that converted to a full board election at the August 2025 annual general meeting. Accel's presence signalled that sophisticated enterprise-technology investors had underwritten the transition from restructuring story to operating-business story.

Orbis Investments, the South African-rooted global value manager, added a different dimension. Orbis's capital profile — patient, multi-year, drawn to structural re-ratings rather than momentum — suggested the placement was attracting investors whose time horizon matched the construction cycle rather than the quarterly earnings cadence. For a company planning $16–20 billion in FY2026 capital expenditure, long-duration equity capital from a value-oriented institution carried different implications than speculative growth allocation.

Nvidia's role has been discussed above. The combination of the three produced a $700 million placement that was simultaneously a strategic validation, a supplier-alignment signal, and a capital-structure reinforcement — arriving at the precise moment when Nebius was beginning its most aggressive infrastructure ramp.

## Positioned but Not Moated

The competitive framing for Nebius at the May 2026 snapshot date required intellectual honesty about the nature of its advantages.

| Operator | Status | Balance Sheet | Nvidia Alignment | Power (Active) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nebius (NBIS) | Public, NASDAQ | $3.7B cash | Strategic equity investor | 170MW → 800-1,000MW guided |
| CoreWeave (CRWV) | Public, NASDAQ | More leveraged | Deep procurement relationship | Larger active footprint |
| Lambda | Private | VC-backed | Nvidia-aligned | Undisclosed |
| Crusoe | Private | VC-backed | Nvidia-aligned | Differentiated (flared-gas power) |
| Azure AI / GCP / AWS | Internal divisions | Balance-sheet unlimited | Preferred customer status | Multi-gigawatt at scale |

Nebius was differentiated by the cash position and by the formalised Nvidia equity alignment. Those were real advantages. They were not irreplaceable moats. CoreWeave had a larger active deployment base. The hyperscalers had unlimited capital and existing customer relationships. Lambda and Crusoe were competing for the same AI-lab customers in overlapping geographies. Vultr and DigitalOcean Nimbus addressed the smaller-scale end of the market but were not structurally comparable at the contracted-ARR level Nebius was playing at.

The structural observation that mattered was this: the case for Nebius's FY2026 revenue and ARR targets rested on three things executing concurrently — GPU allocations arriving on the cadence implied by the Nvidia relationship, power infrastructure commissioning at the rate required to support the 800–1,000 megawatt target, and the contracted customer base remaining in place and drawing against its committed obligations. Each of those was plausible on the available evidence. None was guaranteed. The FY2026 guidance window — the most aggressive capacity-build target in the public AI-cloud peer set — was simultaneously the company's strongest commercial signal and its most demanding operational test. The cash, the contracts, and the Nvidia equity stake had created the conditions for the ramp. Whether the physical infrastructure could be built fast enough to honour those conditions was the year's defining question.

chapters.title: Where Nebius sits in the AI cloud landscape
chapters.body:
The AI infrastructure market that Nebius entered under its new identity in 2024 was already contested, capital-intensive, and structurally stratified. Three distinct competitive tiers had formed by the time the company posted its fourth-quarter 2025 results: the hyperscalers commanding the top of the market through integrated cloud platforms of oceanic scale; a mid-tier of pure-play AI GPU clouds that had accumulated Nvidia hardware and customer contracts ahead of general enterprise demand; and a lower tier of regional or specialty operators seeking to monetise discrete geographic or power advantages. Nebius, with $3.7 billion of cash and a $1.25 billion annualised-revenue run-rate at year-end 2025, sat squarely in the second tier — but the ambition encoded in its guidance placed it on a trajectory designed to compress that distance.

## The Three-Tier Landscape

The top tier belongs to Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Amazon Web Services. These are not competitors Nebius confronted directly for the same customer dollar, at least not in a symmetric sense. The hyperscalers' AI cloud capacity was embedded inside broader cloud relationships that included data storage, managed databases, identity, productivity software, and decades of enterprise integration. A Nebius customer bought AI GPU compute. A Microsoft Azure customer bought AI GPU compute alongside everything else. The competitive pressure from the hyperscaler tier was therefore a form of gravitational field rather than a head-to-head battle: it set the price floor, the service-level expectations, and the default procurement option for the largest enterprises.

The regional and specialty tier — Foxconn-FII's cloud manufacturing partnerships, Equinix's AI Labs offering, and the national-champion clouds operated by Telefónica, Orange, and Deutsche Telekom subsidiaries — occupied a different competitive space. Their advantages were geographic proximity to regulated data jurisdictions (GDPR, DORA, NIS2), local language support, and pre-existing carrier relationships. Their disadvantage was GPU allocation: without Nvidia's direct strategic alignment, access to the newest accelerator generations — H200, B200, the Rubin family — flowed later, in smaller quantities, and at higher cost.

The operative contest for Nebius in 2025 and into 2026 was the middle tier: the pure-play AI GPU clouds. This was the tier in which capital deployment speed, Nvidia relationship depth, data centre power, and customer contract quality determined who would survive the consolidation that analysts across the infrastructure sector expected to arrive by 2027.

## The Pure-Play Peer Set

At the snapshot date of May 2026, the principal competitors in the pure-play AI GPU cloud tier were CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV), Lambda (private), Crusoe (private), and Vultr (private). Each had assembled Nvidia GPU clusters, built or leased data centre capacity, and competed for the same population of AI-lab and enterprise-ML customers whose workloads were too large for consumer cloud and too specialised for the hyperscaler's commoditised instances.

| Company | Status | Balance-sheet posture | Nvidia relationship | Active capacity (est.) | ARR visibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CoreWeave | Public (CRWV) | Highly leveraged; asset-backed debt against GPU collateral | Strategic alignment; among largest Nvidia customers | Larger than Nebius at snapshot | Large contracted backlog |
| **Nebius** | **Public (NBIS)** | **$3.7B cash; low leverage** | **Equity investor (Aug 2025 $700M placement)** | **170MW exit-2025** | **>50% of $7–9B FY26 ARR contracted** |
| Lambda | Private | VC-backed; undisclosed | Nvidia-aligned | Undisclosed | Undisclosed |
| Crusoe | Private | VC-backed; differentiated power strategy | Nvidia-aligned | Undisclosed | Undisclosed |
| Vultr | Private | Founder-owned; bootstrapped origins | Standard procurement | Smaller scale | Undisclosed |

The comparison with CoreWeave crystallised the two dominant models within the pure-play tier. CoreWeave, which completed its own NASDAQ listing in early 2025, had built its scale earlier and faster — benefiting from a head start in GPU procurement and a strategy of financing GPU clusters through asset-backed credit facilities, treating Nvidia hardware as collateral in the same way aircraft lessors treat jet engines. By the snapshot date, CoreWeave's active deployed capacity exceeded Nebius's 170 megawatts materially. But the debt load that funded that build-out distinguished the two balance sheets sharply.

Nebius entered 2026 with $3.7 billion in cash and, by management's account, an $834 million fourth-quarter operating cash flow figure that reflected [customer prepayment dynamics](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) consistent with multi-year enterprise contracting: customers paid ahead of recognised revenue, generating cash on hand in excess of the quarterly revenue line. CoreWeave's balance sheet carried a structurally different risk profile — GPU collateralisation is defensible while Nvidia hardware commands premium secondhand values, but that premium is not guaranteed across hardware generations as depreciation curves steepen and next-generation products arrive.

Both companies shared the most consequential structural fact in the pure-play tier: Nvidia's direct alignment. For Nebius, that alignment was formalised through equity ownership. Nvidia participated in the [oversubscribed $700 million strategic equity placement](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-announces-oversubscribed-strategic-equity-financing-of-usd-700-million-to-accelerate-roll-out-of-full-stack-ai-infrastructure) completed in August 2025, alongside Accel and Orbis Investments.
